## Walkthrough: the click 8.2.1 / PYSEC-2026-2132 case, run through the new runbook

Recorded as the material for the `[operator-attested]` acceptance criterion. This
replays the original incident against `docs/dependency-advisory-runbook.md` as
written, step by step, and states where each detour would have been cut off.

**What actually happened.** PYSEC-2026-2132 was published against `click` 8.2.1,
which `uv.lock` pinned because `inspect-ai` (an `[agents]`-extra dependency)
capped it. uv's universal resolution locks every extra jointly, so the base scan
saw the capped version too. Six changes across five work streams went red
simultaneously. Each author independently: (1) tried `recheck`; (2) tried
`uv lock --upgrade-package click` and saw nothing move; (3) reached for
`constraint-dependencies` to test whether the upgrade was even feasible, got
UNSATISFIABLE, and recorded the conclusion that the upgrade was impossible —
which was wrong.

**Step 1 — "Is this mine?"** Five of the six changes touched no dependency file
at all. Under the new lane rule their Verified gate stays GREEN and prints the
advisory as a warning naming the scheduled canary as owner. Five of the six
diagnostic efforts never start. This is the largest single saving and it is
structural, not advice.

**Step 2 — "Real finding, or flake?"** The runbook states up front that only a
DB-unreachable failure is recheckable and that `recheck` can NEVER clear a real
finding, and the gate's own output distinguishes the two cases in words. The
`recheck` attempt — everyone's first instinct, and the property the ticket
records as the single most time-wasting — is cut off at the first read.

**Step 3 — severity.** PYSEC advisories carry no severity through pip-audit. The
runbook's table says unrated is treated as HIGH and therefore fails, so the
author is not left wondering whether an unrated finding "counts". No detour.

**Step 4 — remediation.** (a) says upgrade the direct dependency first; click is
not a direct dependency of rebar, so this is answered in one line. (b) is the
upstream-cap branch, and it names all three false-progress moves BEFORE
suggesting anything: `uv lock --upgrade-package` is a no-op against a cap;
`constraint-dependencies` can only NARROW and returns UNSATISFIABLE as its
EXPECTED output, which "reads exactly like proof that the upgrade is impossible
— it proves nothing"; and neither is evidence the cap is real. It then names
`override-dependencies` as the correct instrument and gives the exact
`[tool.uv]` block, with the justification naming the advisory (PYSEC-2026-2132),
the capping package (inspect-ai), and the safety argument, plus a REMOVE-WHEN
line.

**Conclusion.** The runbook leads to `override-dependencies` on the first pass
for the one author who owns the lock, and to "not yours" immediately for the
other five. The confidently-recorded wrong conclusion — that UNSATISFIABLE
proved the upgrade impossible — is pre-empted by name rather than left to be
rediscovered. The one thing the runbook does NOT do is decide whether the
inspect-ai cap was stale; it requires evidence (an upstream issue/PR showing the
incompatibility was fixed, plus the capped package importing and running under
the newer version), which is the judgment call that should stay with a person.

**Caveat on scope, for the attesting operator.** This is a replay against the
recorded facts of the incident, not a re-execution of it — the advisory is no
longer outstanding, so the end-to-end path (red canary → filed ticket →
override → cleared → auto-closed ticket) is proven by the unit/wiring suites
rather than by a live occurrence. The first real advisory after this lands is
the true end-to-end test.
